title: Samantha Brought a Shotgun to the Wedding. Maa Inti Bangaaram Lands Friday — and She Produced It Herself.
excerpt: The 'perfect daughter-in-law' has a body count. Samantha Ruth Prabhu's first film as a producer reunites her with the director who made Oh! Baby — and lets her do saree-clad combat with no body double.
body:
The trailer opens like a hundred Telugu family dramas you've half-watched on a Sunday: a nervous new bride, a houseful of in-laws sizing her up, a wedding being planned, the air thick with passive-aggressive comparisons. And then **Samantha Ruth Prabhu** picks up a double-barrelled shotgun, and the genre quietly detonates.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=B9d-wISnm8s</youtube>

**Maa Inti Bangaaram** — "The Gold of Our House" — hits theatres worldwide this Friday, June 19, and it is the most personal swing of Samantha's career. Not because of the action, though there's plenty. Because for the first time, her name sits in the producer's chair. This is her banner, **Tralala Moving Pictures**, putting out its maiden production, with Samantha co-producing alongside her husband, filmmaker **Raj Nidimoru**, and Himank Reddy Duvvuru.

> "What I loved about Maa Inti Bangaaram is that it refuses to put women into boxes. It takes someone people may underestimate and turns her into the most powerful force in the room." — Samantha Ruth Prabhu

That line could double as a thesis for where Samantha is right now. She has spent the last few years refusing every box the industry tried to seal her into, and here she is funding the refusal herself.

## The housewife who fights back

The premise is deliciously sly. Samantha plays a homemaker who married against her in-laws' wishes and arrives, two years later, to finally win them over. Every gesture is scrutinised. Can she be the *perfect* daughter-in-law? And then her past comes knocking, and the dormant skills come out — the ones that turn a soft-spoken newlywed into a lethal protector.

Director **BV Nandini Reddy** stages it as a juxtaposition: domestic life against warrior instinct, a striking portrait of Goddess Kali looming over household squabbles. The action — choreographed by Lee Whittaker and Aejaz Gulab — is gritty and close-quarters, and Samantha reportedly performed several sequences in a saree without a body double. There is a particular thrill in watching a woman fight in six yards of silk and refuse to apologise for either the silk or the fighting.

The title carries a sting Raj Nidimoru, the creator best known for *The Family Man*, is happy to explain.

> "When we call a daughter-in-law 'bangaram' (gold), it doesn't just signify affection, but also hints at control and possessiveness. There is a deeper, darker side to owning somebody." — Raj Nidimoru

That's the film in a sentence: the way families gild the women they also cage. It marks Raj's first professional collaboration with Samantha since their marriage, and the creative chemistry shows in how thoroughly the genre subverts itself.

## A reunion that already struck gold

Samantha and Nandini Reddy last worked together on the 2019 charmer *Oh! Baby*, one of the warmest hits of either woman's career. The reunion alone makes this a must-watch for anyone who remembers how that film balanced comedy and ache. Add **Santhosh Narayanan**'s pulsating score, cinematography by Om Prakash, and a supporting cast featuring **Gulshan Devaiah**, Diganth, Sree Mukhi and Gautami, and the technical pedigree is serious.

The film originally targeted May 15 but shifted to June 19 to dodge the IPL 2026 frenzy — a strategic call to let Telugu audiences ride out the Sunrisers Hyderabad campaign before heading to the cinema. Smart. Nobody wins a box-office war against cricket.

## Where the diaspora can watch

Maa Inti Bangaaram releases theatrically in Telugu first, and given Tralala's worldwide framing, expect overseas screens across the US, UK and Canada through the usual Telugu-cinema distributors — the same circuits that turned recent Samantha and Daggubati-family releases into NRI weekend events. For diaspora fans who can't make opening weekend, a streaming premiere will almost certainly follow within weeks; watch this space for the OTT and dub-language confirmation.

Here's the thing worth saying plainly: Samantha didn't need to produce her own film. She is one of the most bankable stars in Indian cinema. She chose to, because the role she wanted — the underestimated woman who turns out to be the most dangerous person in the house — is exactly the kind of part the industry rarely hands a leading lady. So she handed it to herself.

This GOLD, as the makers keep teasing, is bloody bold. Come Friday, we find out just how bold.
